title: Blog 1
content:
SESSION POLICIES IN AMAZON EKS POD IDENTITY Amazon EKS Pod Identity has recently added the session policies feature, allowing you to narrow IAM permissions flexibly and precisely for each pod without needing to create many separate IAM roles. This is an important step forward that helps apply the principle of least privilege more effectively in large-scale Kubernetes environments.
Key points to know:
A session policy is an inline IAM policy specified when creating or updating a Pod Identity association. Effective permissions = intersection between the IAM role permissions and the session policy → the session policy can only narrow permissions, not expand them. Helps avoid over-permissioning when reusing a single IAM role for multiple workloads with different needs. Supports both same-account and cross-account (via IAM role chaining). Significantly reduces the number of IAM roles that need to be managed, helping avoid hitting IAM quota limits in large clusters. Easily configured through the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, or AWS SDK when creating an association between a Kubernetes ServiceAccount and an IAM role. This feature is especially useful when you have many applications running on the same IAM role but need different permission restrictions (for example: one pod only reads a specific S3 bucket, another pod only calls certain APIs).

title: Proposal
content:
WEB TRAVEL PLATFORM ON CLOUD High-Availability and Auto-Scaling AWS Architecture Solution for Online Tour Booking Systems 1. Executive Summary Web Travel Platform is designed and deployed to modernize online tour management, searching, and booking systems on the Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud platform. The system operates reliably in a live cloud environment with flexible auto-scaling capabilities ranging from 0 to a maximum of 3 application servers depending on incoming traffic. The platform leverages core AWS services (VPC, EC2, RDS, Auto Scaling) to ensure high availability, strict data isolation, and operational cost optimization within the 100 USD AWS Promotional Credits budget.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Traditional web applications deployed on a single physical server or local environment (such as XAMPP) frequently experience overloading during peak tourism seasons when user traffic surges. Hosting both web source code and the database on the same server increases the risk of data breaches, complicates backup and recovery procedures, and introduces a Single Point of Failure (SPOF).
The Solution The platform utilizes Amazon VPC to segment the network infrastructure into public and private tiers across two Availability Zones. The application tier runs on Amazon EC2 (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) hosting PHP source code, integrated with an Auto Scaling Group and a custom AMI template to automatically replicate servers when needed. The data tier is migrated to the managed Amazon RDS (MySQL) service, completely isolated inside a Private Subnet and protected by two layers of Security Groups.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution completely eliminates upfront physical server hardware investment and maintenance costs while enhancing system reliability and customer data security. Actual operational costs are kept minimal (nearly 0 USD when stopped in standby mode and approximately 0.025 USD/hour when both EC2 and RDS are active), fitting comfortably within the 100 USD Credits academic grant. The system significantly reduces manual infrastructure administration overhead and is ready for immediate enterprise-scale expansion.
3. Solution Architecture The platform adopts a standard multi-tier AWS cloud architecture in the Singapore Region (ap-southeast-1). The entire infrastructure resides within a custom Virtual Private Cloud named travel-vpc, spanning two Availability Zones (ap-southeast-1a and ap-southeast-1b). The web server Web-travel-sv is placed inside a Public Subnet, receiving user traffic through an Internet Gateway and the TL-Web security group. Business data is queried internally from travel-database (Amazon RDS MySQL) located in a Private Subnet protected by the TL-Database security group. The Travel-auto-scaling-group, combined with Web-Travel-AMI and Travel-target, guarantees elastic scalability and continuous user session persistence.
4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project was executed over 10 weeks (conducted regularly every Saturday) across four primary phases:
Survey and Source Code Standardization (Weeks 1 – 2): Tested the Web Travel application locally on XAMPP, exported the travel_test.sql database dump, and established centralized version control on GitHub (dt-kien04/du-an-01). Network and Security Setup (Weeks 3 – 4): Provisioned travel-vpc, segmented 2 Public Subnets and 2 Private Subnets, and configured the TL-Web and TL-Database security groups. Database and Web Server Deployment (Weeks 5 – 7): Launched Amazon RDS (travel-database), provisioned the Ubuntu EC2 instance (Web-travel-sv), installed the LAMP stack, cloned source code from GitHub, and established database connectivity. Auto-Scaling Configuration and Operational Optimization (Weeks 8 – 10): Packaged Web-Travel-AMI, configured the Target Group (Travel-target), Launch Template (Travel-template), and Auto Scaling Group, and finalized the graduation thesis documentation. Technical Requirements Application Tier (Web Tier): Amazon EC2 t3.micro virtual instance running Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS, configured with Apache2, PHP 8.x, MySQL Client, and Git. Remote administrative access is authenticated via an SSH Key Pair (khoa-travel.pem). Data Tier (Database Tier): Amazon RDS running MySQL Community Edition on a db.t4g.micro instance with 20 GiB SSD (gp2) storage, public access disabled (Public access = No), and a 1-day automated backup retention period.
5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline Preparation Phase (Weeks 1 – 2): Studied AWS cloud fundamentals, activated the 100 Credits account, standardized PHP source code, and pushed the repository to GitHub.
8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Successfully deliver a stable, live online tour booking platform on the AWS cloud featuring a highly secure multi-tier network architecture, eliminating single points of failure and enabling seamless auto-scaling under high traffic loads.
Long-term Value Establish a standardized cloud architecture foundation ready for future enterprise upgrades, including offloading static image assets to Amazon S3 + CloudFront, integrating a custom domain via Amazon Route 53 with HTTPS (ACM) encryption, and automating deployments via CI/CD pipelines.

Report on the Mini Meetup – First Cloud AI Journey 1. Event Objectives The Mini Meetup – First Cloud AI Journey, held on August 22, 2026, was a knowledge-sharing event organized by the FCAJ community. The event focused on API standards in Backend development, helping participants better understand the role of APIs in building and developing modern software systems.
The main objectives of the event were:
To understand the role of APIs in connecting and exchanging data between system components. To explore important standards and principles for designing Backend APIs. To understand the importance of building APIs that are easy to use, maintain, and scale. To encourage continuous learning, knowledge sharing, and professional development within the technology community. 2. Speaker and Topic Nguyen Nhan – FCAJ Member: API Standards in Backend Development. 3. Key Topics 3.1. Overview of APIs in Backend Development An API (Application Programming Interface) allows applications or software components to communicate and exchange data with one another. In modern systems, APIs play an important role in connecting Frontend applications with Backend services, integrating services, and facilitating data exchange between different systems.
Key concepts include:
Understanding the concept of APIs and their role in software architecture. Recognizing how APIs enable communication between applications and services. Understanding the importance of designing APIs that are clear, consistent, and easy to use. Recognizing the role of APIs in integrating components within larger systems. 3.2. API Design Standards and Principles The session focused on important standards and principles for developing Backend APIs, with an emphasis on usability, maintainability, and scalability as systems grow.
Key aspects include:
Consistency: Using consistent endpoint naming conventions, data structures, and response formats. Usability: Designing clear endpoints that other applications and services can easily integrate with. Maintainability: Organizing APIs logically to simplify updates, bug fixes, and the development of new features. Scalability: Designing APIs with a structure that can accommodate future system growth. Compatibility: Minimizing breaking changes that could affect applications already using the APIs. These principles demonstrate that API development involves more than simply processing requests. It also requires attention to design quality and long-term maintainability.
3.3. The Role of APIs in Modern Systems As software systems become more complex, APIs become essential components that enable services to communicate and work together. Well-designed APIs can reduce dependencies between components, support integration, and facilitate future system development.
Important considerations when designing APIs include:
Clearly defining the purpose of each endpoint and the data it needs to exchange. Standardizing request handling, responses, and error messages. Prioritizing authentication, authorization, and data protection when exposing APIs. Considering API versioning when modifying or introducing new features. Providing clear API documentation to support development and integration. These principles can be applied when designing and developing software systems in real-world environments.
4. Knowledge and Skills Gained 4.1. Technical Knowledge APIs and Backend Development: Gained a better understanding of the role of APIs in connecting software system components. API Design: Recognized the importance of consistency, usability, and maintainability. System Integration: Learned more about how APIs facilitate communication and data exchange between applications and services. API Security: Recognized the need for authentication, authorization, and data protection when developing service interfaces. Scalability: Understood that API design should accommodate future system growth and changing requirements. 4.2. Personal Development Skills Improved my ability to explore and learn new technical concepts. Understood the value of sharing technical knowledge and practical experience within a technology community. Gained further motivation to explore API design, documentation, and testing. Recognized the importance of continuous learning in keeping up with the development of modern systems. 5. Application to My Internship Project My internship project is titled “Design and Implementation of a Hybrid Cloud System Connecting Multi-Branch Enterprise Networks Using Site-to-Site VPN with Centralized Monitoring.”
Although the main focus of my project is network infrastructure and cloud computing, knowledge of APIs can support the management and integration of services within the system in several ways:
AWS Services: Explore how AWS services provide APIs for managing cloud resources and performing operations programmatically. System Integration: Understand the role of APIs in connecting applications and services related to the Hybrid Cloud environment. Centralized Monitoring: Investigate how monitoring tools expose APIs for retrieving data, integrating information, or automating certain operations when needed. Security and Access Management: Pay attention to authentication, authorization, and information protection when services exchange data. Automation: Expand my knowledge of APIs to explore opportunities for automating cloud resource management in future development stages. These topics provide a broader perspective on the relationship between software development, service management, and cloud infrastructure operations.
6. Event Experience Participating in the Mini Meetup – First Cloud AI Journey on August 22, 2026, gave me an opportunity to explore APIs in Backend development and better understand an important aspect of modern system design.
Through the topic shared by Nguyen Nhan, I gained further insight into API design principles, particularly consistency, maintainability, and scalability. These factors are essential for enabling software components to communicate effectively as systems grow in complexity.
In addition to the technical content, the knowledge-sharing spirit among FCAJ members was another valuable aspect of the event. It encouraged participants to learn proactively, exchange experiences, and contribute knowledge to the community.
7. Conclusion and Lessons Learned Through the Mini Meetup – First Cloud AI Journey on August 22, 2026, I gained a better understanding of how APIs connect and integrate services in modern systems. API design should prioritize consistency, usability, security, maintainability, and scalability.
Furthermore, the meetup helped me recognize the value of continuous learning and knowledge sharing within the technology community. The knowledge gained provides a foundation for further exploring APIs, understanding how AWS services interact, and investigating the potential integration of APIs into Hybrid Cloud management and monitoring.

title: Test the Interface Endpoint
content:
Get the regional DNS name of S3 interface endpoint From the Amazon VPC menu, choose Endpoints.
Click the name of newly created endpoint: s3-interface-endpoint. Click details and save the regional DNS name of the endpoint (the first one) to your text-editor for later use.
Connect to EC2 instance in “VPC On-prem” Navigate to Session manager by typing “session manager” in the search box
Click Start Session, and select the EC2 instance named Test-Interface-Endpoint. This EC2 instance is running in “VPC On-prem” and will be used to test connectivty to Amazon S3 through the Interface endpoint we just created. Session Manager will open a new browser tab with a shell prompt: sh-4.2 $
Change to the ssm-user’s home directory with command “cd ~”
Create a file named testfile2.xyz
fallocate -l 1G testfile2.xyz Copy file to the same S3 bucket we created in section 3.2 aws s3 cp --endpoint-url https://bucket.<Regional-DNS-Name> testfile2.xyz s3://<your-bucket-name> This command requires the –endpoint-url parameter, because you need to use the endpoint-specific DNS name to access S3 using an Interface endpoint. Do not include the leading ’ * ’ when copying/pasting the regional DNS name. Provide your S3 bucket name created earlier Now the file has been added to your S3 bucket. Let check your S3 bucket in the next step.
Check Object in S3 bucket Navigate to S3 console Click Buckets Click the name of your bucket and you will see testfile2.xyz has been added to your bucket

title: Meeting 3
content:
Investigation Series – Learn, Build, Share, Grow 1. Event Objectives FCAJ Mini Meetup – From Learning to Building, held on October 25, 2026, was a knowledge-sharing event organized by the First Cloud AI Journey community. The event focused on the topic Cloud Quest – An Interactive AWS Learning Platform for Vietnamese Learners, helping participants gain insights into how acquired knowledge can be transformed into a technology product with practical value.
Through the presentation by Nguyễn Minh Toàn, participants had the opportunity to learn about the research and development journey of Cloud Quest, from the initial idea to the process of building an interactive learning platform with various components.
The main objectives of the event included:
Understanding the idea and development goals of the Cloud Quest project. Exploring how to build an interactive AWS learning platform that is more accessible to Vietnamese learners. Learning about the development of interactive 3D models, simulated labs, quizzes, and flashcards. Understanding how to transform acquired knowledge into a technology project with practical value. Encouraging a proactive learning mindset, hands-on practice, product development, and knowledge sharing within the community. 2. Speaker and Presentation Topic Nguyễn Minh Toàn – FCAJ Member | PTIT: Cloud Quest – An Interactive AWS Learning Platform for Vietnamese Learners. 3. Key Highlights 3.1. Overview of the Cloud Quest Project Cloud Quest is a personal project researched and developed by Nguyễn Minh Toàn with the goal of helping learners approach AWS knowledge in a more visual and understandable way.
Instead of relying solely on theoretical documentation, the project aims to combine various interactive learning methods to help learners acquire knowledge and better visualize concepts related to cloud computing.
Some of the project’s main objectives include:
Building a platform that helps learners approach AWS knowledge visually. Creating an interactive learning environment through 3D models. Integrating simulated labs to support hands-on learning. Incorporating quizzes and flashcards to reinforce knowledge after learning. Making AWS more accessible and easier to understand for Vietnamese learners. The project demonstrates that technology learning does not necessarily have to be limited to documentation and theory. It can also be expanded through educational products developed by learners themselves.
3.2. Research and Development Process of Cloud Quest One of the highlights of the presentation was the journey of developing Cloud Quest from an initial idea into a project with multiple interactive components.
This process demonstrates the combination of technical knowledge, research capabilities, and product development skills.
The notable components involved in building the project include:
Interactive 3D Models: Creating a visual environment that helps learners explore AWS concepts through 3D models. Simulated Labs: Developing simulated learning activities to help learners visualize and understand how AWS services work. Quizzes: Integrating multiple-choice questions to help learners evaluate their understanding and reinforce their knowledge. Flashcards: Using digital flashcards to support the review and memorization of important concepts and knowledge. Learning Content Integration: Combining these components into a structured and interactive learning platform. Through the development process of Cloud Quest, it becomes clear that building a technology product requires more than theoretical knowledge. Developers need to identify problems, research solutions, build features, and continuously improve their products.
3.3. From Learning to Building Real-World Products The topic From Learning to Building emphasizes the importance of transforming acquired knowledge into products with practical value.
In technology learning, understanding fundamental knowledge is essential. However, the ability to apply that knowledge to solve problems and develop products also plays a very important role.
Some valuable lessons from the Cloud Quest development journey include:
Proactive Research: Going beyond existing knowledge by actively exploring and researching new ideas. Learning Through Practice: Applying acquired knowledge to develop specific features and functionalities. Product Development Mindset: Identifying objectives, target users, and the value that a product aims to deliver. Continuous Improvement: Gradually developing, testing, and improving the product throughout the implementation process. Knowledge Sharing: Bringing research results and developed products to the community to encourage learning and collaboration. These lessons demonstrate a proactive learning mindset, in which learners should not simply acquire knowledge but also know how to apply it and create value from what they have learned.
4. Knowledge and Skills Acquired 4.1. Technical Knowledge Cloud Computing: Gaining a better understanding of how to build a learning platform that supports access to AWS knowledge. Product Development: Understanding the basic stages of transforming an idea into a developed and completed personal project. Interactive 3D Models: Learning about the potential application of 3D models in visualizing technical concepts. Practical Simulations: Understanding the role of simulated labs in helping learners acquire knowledge through hands-on practice. Learning Support Tools: Exploring how quizzes and flashcards can be used to reinforce and memorize knowledge more effectively. 4.2. Personal Development Skills Improving proactive thinking when researching and exploring new technologies. Learning how to transform ideas into products with specific functions and objectives. Recognizing the importance of combining theoretical knowledge with practical experience. Developing problem-solving skills throughout the process of building and improving a project. Understanding the value of sharing experiences and personal projects with the technology community. 5. Application to My Internship Project My internship project is “Design and Implementation of a Hybrid Cloud System Connecting a Multi-Branch Enterprise Network Using Site-to-Site VPN Integrated with a Centralized Monitoring Solution”.
Although Cloud Quest focuses on developing an AWS learning platform, the knowledge and experience shared during the meetup can still be applied to my research and development process in several ways:
Proactive AWS Research: Continuing to explore AWS services, cloud architecture, and system deployment through a combination of documentation and hands-on practice. Hands-on System Development: Applying acquired knowledge to deploy practical components such as VPC, EC2, Site-to-Site VPN, and monitoring solutions. System Simulation: Using EVE-NG to build a multi-branch enterprise network model, test connectivity, and evaluate the operation of the Hybrid Cloud system. Building a Practical Product: Approaching the internship project not merely as a theoretical research topic but as a product that needs to be designed, deployed, tested, and improved. Sharing Results: Documenting the deployment process, configurations, and lessons learned to create technical guides and share knowledge with the community. These lessons motivate me to actively research, practice, and improve my Hybrid Cloud system rather than simply stopping at understanding cloud computing concepts.
6. Experience Participating in the Event Participating in FCAJ Mini Meetup – From Learning to Building on October 25, 2026, was an opportunity for me to gain practical insights into the process of developing a technology project from an initial idea into a completed product.
Through Nguyễn Minh Toàn’s presentation about Cloud Quest, I gained a better understanding that learning AWS should not be limited to reading documentation or completing existing labs. It can also be expanded into personal projects that bring value to other learners.
In particular, combining interactive 3D models, simulated labs, quizzes, and flashcards within a single platform demonstrates creativity in approaching and delivering technical knowledge.
Besides the technical content, what impressed me was the proactive research and product development mindset demonstrated by a member of the FCAJ community. This also motivates me to continue developing my internship project, gaining practical experience, and gradually improving my professional skills.
7. Conclusion and Lessons Learned Through FCAJ Mini Meetup – From Learning to Building on October 25, 2026, I realized that technology learning and research should be closely connected with practical experience and the ability to create real-world products.
Nguyễn Minh Toàn’s Cloud Quest project is an example of how knowledge can be transformed into a valuable product through research, creativity, and persistent development. The combination of interactive 3D models, simulated labs, quizzes, and flashcards also introduces a new approach to learning and acquiring AWS knowledge.
The most important lesson I learned from this meetup is that I should not stop at learning and exploring knowledge. Instead, I need to actively apply what I have learned to build, test, and improve practical products.
This is also the spirit that the FCAJ community aims to promote: Not just learning, but also practicing, building, and sharing what we have accomplished with the community.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Workshop
content:
DEPLOYING A HIGH-AVAILABILITY AND AUTO-SCALING WEB TRAVEL APPLICATION ON AWS Overview Modern cloud architecture resolves the overloading and Single Point of Failure (SPOF) challenges of traditional physical servers by clearly decoupling the networking, application, and database tiers.
In this lab, we will learn how to design, configure, and operate a complete infrastructure on AWS for the Web Travel online tour booking application (PHP/MySQL). The system is deployed within an isolated multi-Availability Zone (Multi-AZ) environment, ensuring robust data security and seamless auto-scaling capabilities when user traffic surges.
We will build and integrate three core service layers to operate an enterprise-standard web application:
Virtual Private Cloud & Security (Amazon VPC & Security Groups) - Provision the travel-vpc network infrastructure separating Public Subnets and Private Subnets, strictly controlling traffic via two firewall layers: TL-Web and TL-Database. Managed Database Service (Amazon RDS) - Deploy a MySQL database (travel-database) completely isolated inside a Private Subnet to safeguard business data and communicate internally with the application server. Application Server & Auto Scaling (EC2, AMI & Auto Scaling) – Host the source code on an Ubuntu EC2 instance (Web-travel-sv), package it into a golden image (Web-Travel-AMI), and configure Travel-auto-scaling-group to dynamically orchestrate compute resources. title: Product Description
content:
Web Travel Platform on AWS Cloud Project Title: Design and Deployment of a High-Availability, Auto-Scaling Online Tour Booking System on AWS
Region: Asia Pacific (Singapore) — ap-southeast-1
Source Code Repository: https://github.com/dt-kien04/du-an-01
1. Problem Statement Traditional web applications hosted on a single on-premises physical server or local development environment (such as XAMPP) face critical operational, security, and scalability challenges:
Traffic Spikes & Server Overloading: During peak holiday and tourism seasons, sudden surges in concurrent users overwhelm single-server architectures, causing slow response times or complete service downtime. Single Point of Failure (SPOF): Hosting both the web application (Apache/PHP) and the relational database (MySQL) on the same server means any hardware failure, OS crash, or resource exhaustion brings down the entire platform. Security & Data Exposure Risks: Exposing a server directly without strict network segmentation puts sensitive customer records, user credentials, and tour booking data at risk. Additionally, default development settings (such as displaying verbose PHP error traces) can leak internal directory structures. High Upfront Capital Expenditure & Rigid Scaling: Purchasing physical server hardware requires significant upfront investment and manual provisioning, making it inefficient to scale resources up during busy periods or down during quiet periods. 2. Proposed Solution To overcome these limitations, the Web Travel Platform is migrated and re-architected onto Amazon Web Services (AWS) using a decoupled, multi-tier, and auto-scaling cloud architecture:
Isolated Multi-AZ Virtual Private Cloud (travel-vpc): Configured a custom VPC (10.0.0.0/16) spanning two Availability Zones (ap-southeast-1a and ap-southeast-1b). Segmented into 2 Public Subnets (for outward-facing web servers) and 2 Private Subnets (to completely isolate the database from direct Internet access), connected via an Internet Gateway (omitting expensive NAT Gateways to optimize budget). Two-Tier Stateful Firewall Security (Security Groups): TL-Web: Allows public web traffic on HTTP (Port 80) and HTTPS (Port 443), while restricting administrative SSH (Port 22) access strictly to the administrator’s personal IP address. TL-Database: Enforces the principle of least privilege by permitting inbound MySQL/Aurora (Port 3306) connections exclusively from instances associated with TL-Web. Managed Relational Database (Amazon RDS): Deployed travel-database (MySQL Community Edition on db.t4g.micro with 20 GiB gp2 SSD) inside a Private Subnet Group (travel-data-subnet-group) with Public access = No and automated daily backups. Elastic Compute & Auto Scaling (EC2, AMI, Target Group, Auto Scaling Group): Hosted the PHP/Apache application on Web-travel-sv (t3.micro, Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS). Captured the production-ready server into a golden image (Web-Travel-AMI). Configured a Target Group (Travel-target) with Stickiness (Sticky Sessions) enabled to preserve user login states, paired with a Launch Template (Travel-template) and an Auto Scaling Group (Travel-auto-scaling-group) capable of scaling between 0 and 3 instances. 3. End-to-End Workflow Phase 1: Source Code Preparation & Version Control Tested and validated the Web Travel application (index.php, css/, html/, photo/, php/, view/) locally on XAMPP. Exported the standardized relational database schema and initial records (users, tours, dat_cho) into travel_test.sql. Pushed the entire codebase and SQL dump to the centralized GitHub repository (dt-kien04/du-an-01). Phase 2: Network & Security Infrastructure Provisioning Created travel-vpc (10.0.0.0/16) across ap-southeast-1a and ap-southeast-1b with 2 Public Subnets (auto-assign public IPv4 enabled), 2 Private Subnets, Route Tables, and an Internet Gateway. Configured TL-Web and TL-Database Security Groups to isolate database traffic from external networks. Phase 3: Database & Application Server Deployment Provisioned travel-database on Amazon RDS (db.t4g.micro) inside the Private Subnets and retrieved its internal connection Endpoint (travel-database.c7o8imgka428.ap-southeast-1.rds.amazonaws.com). Generated the SSH key pair (khoa-travel.pem, chmod 400) and launched Web-travel-sv (t3.micro, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) inside Public Subnet 1. Connected via SSH from VS Code Terminal, installed the LAMP stack (apache2, php, libapache2-mod-php, php-mysql, mysql-client, git), cleared /var/www/html/, cloned the code from GitHub, and set ownership (www-data) for the photo/ directory. Imported travel_test.sql into Amazon RDS via the MySQL CLI and updated /var/www/html/php/ket_noi.php with the RDS Endpoint and credentials. Phase 4: High Availability, Auto Scaling & Operational Hardening Verified live end-to-end user workflows (tour browsing, registration/login, tour booking, and admin dashboard) via the public IPv4 address. Hardened production reliability by troubleshooting runtime connection logs (/var/log/apache2/error.log), disabling public error display (display_errors = Off), and configuring SSH keep-alive settings. Packaged the verified server into Web-Travel-AMI, created Travel-target (with Stickiness enabled), built Travel-template, and launched Travel-auto-scaling-group (Min: 0, Desired: 0, Max: 3). Implemented a cost-control routine to temporarily Stop EC2 and RDS instances when idle. Runtime Request Flow Customer Request: User Browser $ ightarrow$ HTTP (Port 80) $ ightarrow$ Internet Gateway $ ightarrow$ TL-Web $ ightarrow$ EC2 Web Server (Apache/PHP) $ ightarrow$ MySQL (Port 3306) via TL-Database $ ightarrow$ Amazon RDS (Private Subnet). Admin & Deployment Flow: Admin Workstation (MacBook) $ ightarrow$ SSH (Port 22) + khoa-travel.pem $ ightarrow$ EC2 Instance $\leftarrow$ git clone/pull $\leftarrow$ GitHub Repository. 4. Additional (Optional Enhancements) To evolve this architecture into a full enterprise-grade production platform in future iterations, the following optional enhancements are recommended:
Application Load Balancer (ALB): Attach an internet-facing ALB across both Public Subnets in front of Travel-target to evenly distribute incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and perform automated health checks across scaled EC2 instances. Custom Domain & HTTPS Encryption (Route 53 / DuckDNS + ACM / Certbot): Map a friendly domain name to the platform and provision free SSL/TLS certificates to enforce HTTPS (Port 443) encryption and eliminate browser security warnings. Stateless Media Storage (Amazon S3 + CloudFront): Offload tour images from the local EC2 /var/www/html/photo/ directory to an Amazon S3 bucket served via Amazon CloudFront (CDN) so dynamically scaled EC2 instances remain completely stateless. Automated CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions / AWS CodePipeline): Automate code deployment so every git push to the main branch automatically updates the web servers without manual SSH intervention. Performance Load Testing (Apache JMeter): Conduct simulated concurrent user stress tests to benchmark response times and trigger automated CloudWatch alarm scaling policies. 5. Cost Estimation & Optimization The architecture was designed to operate within a 100 USD AWS Promotional Credits academic budget in the Singapore (ap-southeast-1) Region.
Monthly On-Demand Cost Breakdown (Assuming 24/7 Continuous Operation) AWS Service Specification / Configuration Monthly Usage Estimated Cost (USD) Amazon EC2 t3.micro (2 vCPU, 1 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04) 730 hours (24/7) ~$8.47 (Free Tier eligible) Amazon EBS & AMI 8 GiB gp3 Root Volume + 8 GiB AMI Snapshot 16 GiB total ~$1.16 Amazon RDS db.t4g.micro (Single-AZ, MySQL) 730 hours (24/7) ~$11.68 Amazon RDS Storage General Purpose SSD (gp2) 20 GiB ~$2.76 Networking & Scaling VPC, Subnets, IGW, Security Groups, Target Group, ASG Always active $0.00 (Free management) Data Transfer Out Outbound Internet traffic ~1 GB/month $0.00 (First 100 GB free) Total (24/7 Baseline) Continuous full-time operation Full Month ~$24.07 / month Actual Optimized Project Cost Active Hourly Rate: ~$0.025/hour when both Web-travel-sv and travel-database are running simultaneously. Cost-Saving Measures Applied: Avoided NAT Gateway (~$32+/month) by placing web servers in Public Subnets and utilizing an Internet Gateway. Configured Travel-auto-scaling-group with Desired capacity = 0 during idle periods to prevent unintended EC2 launches. Enforced a strict Stop / Stop temporarily routine for EC2 and RDS immediately after development and testing sessions. Net Credit Consumption: Under $5.00 USD across the entire 10-week project lifecycle, preserving over 95% of the 100 USD Credits budget.
